source.title: Foong Chee Mun (CEO, YTL AI Labs / CPO, Ryt Bank) says the "AI is coming for engineers" take is too simplistic — and his own headcount numbers are the receipts
source.description: TL;DR: A CEO looked straight at the "AI is coming for engineers" panic and called it too simple. He didn't say why — not until his own hiring numbers came up. Foong Chee Mun runs AI Labs at YTL and product at Ryt Bank, and when someone hands him the "engineers will just get replaced" line, he doesn't argue with it in the abstract. He points at his own headcount. Same number of engineers, he says, even after the work moved from AI-assisted coding to AI-generated coding — because someone still has to decide whether what the AI wrote is actually right, and that's not typing, that's judgment. Chee Mun gets to say this with a company behind him. You don't have a company behind you saying it. You’re doing the reskilling at night, by yourself, because if you say out loud in front of your team that you’re not sure where you stand, that's not honesty — that's handing them a reason to start doubting you. Chee Mun's data point is real. It's also not yours. THE GAP: Somebody's already proving that judgment gets more valuable, not less, as AI absorbs the typing — the hiring data backs it up, engineering leaders are on record now saying they're hiring for judgment and systems thinking over raw coding speed. The room that's still wide open: nobody's built the thing that takes that macro shift and hands it to the one engineer who needs to see it about his own job, without his employer having to install anything or sign off on anything first. The tools that measure what AI is doing to an engineering org already exist, and so do the tools that tell you what the market pays — they've just never been pointed at the same person's own inbox. The way in isn't to out-build the incumbents at their own game — it's to go around them the way salary-transparency sites did: build trust with the individual first, one anonymous data point at a time, and let the product get built for the engineer instead of for his employer. On the numbers already on the table — nobody's paying for this yet, but the shape of a free, individual-first version has a real 18-to-30-month runway to something worth paying for, the same runway salary-transparency tools needed before they became anything. FEASIBILITY: Opportunity: The room is real — the tools that watch what AI does to an engineering org, and the tools that tell you what you're worth on the market, have never been pointed at the same person at the same time. Specification: Tracks one person's own AI-era review load next to a peer-benchmarked pay comparison — nothing else. No dashboards for a boss. No integration a company has to approve. Roadmap: · Launch free and anonymous — no employer, no install, just the engineer and the form. · Once enough people are in, layer in the one thing nobody else is asking for: how much of your week now goes to catching what the AI got wrong. · Turn that combination into a one-page brief a person can actually bring into their own review. · Only much later — and only if it makes sense — let a company look at the aggregate. Never the starting point. Top 3 Assumptions: 1. People will tell the truth about their own review load and pay, anonymously, without their employer anywhere near it. Cheapest way to find out: a page that just asks, and see who fills it in. 2. Pay data alone isn't enough to pull someone away from what already exists. Cheapest way to find out: build ten comparisons by hand for real people first, see if they'd actually use them. 3. People can describe their own review burden honestly without anything being wired into their GitHub yet. Cheapest way to find out: just ask them to estimate it themselves, before building anything automatic. Feasibility Snapshot: · Technical — low risk to start; a form and public numbers, nothing that needs an engineering team yet. · Unit Economics — cheap to run at first, the same way every version of this has been cheap to run at first. · Profitability Horizon — a year and a half to two and a half years before there's anything to charge for. · Data-Moat — the longer it runs, the harder it gets to copy, because a company-installed tool can never see what someone won't tell their company. · Legal-Compliance — lighter than most, since nothing is wired into an employer's own systems; still needs the same anonymity safeguards every pay-transparency tool needs. MVP Definition: Someone tells it what their week actually looks like and what they're paid. It hands back one page showing where they stand against people like them. They decide what to do with it — nobody decides for them. It never touches a company's own systems, and it never pretends to replace an actual performance review. Go-To-Market: Starts with the people already having this exact conversation with each other in public — the same rooms where this kind of anxiety already lives. Grows the way every honest pay-transparency tool has grown: person to person, not company to company. The pitch against what's already out there isn't complicated — the existing tools tell you what you're worth; this is the first one that also tells you why, right now, this year. Financing: The companies already doing half of this aren't struggling for money — tens of millions raised, one of them bought outright for a billion dollars last year. None of that capital is required to start this. It starts on nothing, the same way the pay-transparency sites people already trust started on nothing. Decision Gate: The real test isn't revenue on day one — it's whether enough people trust it with their own numbers that the data itself becomes worth something to somebody bigger down the line. That's the same gate the last big acquisition in this exact space cleared. _____________________________________ I remember back in my days working for one of the largest construction firms in Malaysia, circa 2007 or so. One day, I overhead a conversation between my Senior QAQC Manager, K. and the Project Director, C. C. was in a hurry. But K. caught him, trying to explain his case. I can see K was exacerbated — like he's trying not to take the blame kind of exacerbated. It appeared that K was talking about us taking over a mega project that was half-way abandoned. Details were sketchy at best. But K gave the impression that the owner of the project wants to keep this hush hush. The current main contractor did a screwed-up job and the owner fired them from site. Such scenario is kind of detrimental to the reputation for both parties. And understandably, the owner invited us to step in to salvage the project, because we're one of the big boys in town. As I eavesdropped their conversations, I heard C planned to jack up the cost of construction substantially. Why, you ask? Well of course to absorb all the risk of repair and refurbish the abandoned project towards completion. That's why. The previous dirtbag main con can just wipe their ass and moved on. But the owner can't do that. They were under tremendous pressure to meet deadlines, or their bottom-line suffer. C knew all too well. The vulture in C siezed the opportunity to squeeze the owner real hard and he rightly did so. What I'm trying to say is these AI may speed up and streamline our work. But they can't go to jail for us, when they screw up. At the end of the day, human beings are still held liable. These Senior Engineers absorb the risk; they rightly take home the dough. ________________________________________ Every post that goes out of this account keeps landing on the same thing, whatever the guest, whatever the clip: it was never really about the tool. It's about who still gets to say they matter once the tool already works. This one's no exception — Chee Mun's headcount and K.'s liability are the same story told forty years apart. Drop your take — is your own company actually saying any of this out loud, or is it just something you're supposed to figure out on your own?
